Description: The Jewish Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania provides a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary approach to Jewish civilization from antiquity to the present. As an academic field, Jewish studies is anchored in the traditional humanities—in the mastery of languages and the close reading of texts from a wide variety of genres—but it has also come to embrace the full gamut of approaches of the social sciences. The Jewish studies major will provide the basic tools for all students to pursue this inter-disciplinary field while encouraging each to develop his or her specific interests. This major can be an excellent preparation for careers in Jewish education, the rabbinate, Jewish communal service, and graduate work in Jewish studies. For students whose main interests lie elsewhere, a major in Jewish Studies will also constitute a superb liberal arts education and an unusually rich opportunity to explore questions of history, literature, religion, and culture that have broad applicability to other fields.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Latin American & Latinx Studies,
Requirements: First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application, including the Penn Writing Supplement. Required supporting documents include an official high school transcript, a School Report, one counselor recommendation, and two teacher recommendations. A Mid-Year Report must be submitted when first-term/second-quarter senior grades are available, and a Final Report is required for all matriculating students. An interview is optional and not guaranteed.
Description: The Latin American and Latinx Studies (LALS) Program offers an interdisciplinary major and minor to students in the College of Arts and Sciences. LALS offers students the opportunity to learn about the diverse histories, politics, economies, and cultures of the region as well as those of its peoples in the U.S. By combining courses offered in several departments, LALS introduces students to the study of Latin America and the Caribbean, while also providing them with the opportunity to specialize in one or two disciplines and/or one or two areas of the region. A certificate in LALS is available for Wharton undergraduates, and a minor for undergraduates in the Schools of Engineering and Applied Science and Nursing. Penn undergraduates in all four schools can get a language certificate in Portuguese, Quechua or Spanish.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Law and Society,
Requirements: First-year applicants apply for admission to one of Penn’s four undergraduate schools, not to a specific major. The Law and Society major is in the College of Arts and Sciences. General application requirements include: Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir; Penn-specific Essay; Official High School Transcript; School Report; Counselor Recommendation; Two Teacher Recommendations; Mid-Year Report; and a Final Report for admitted students who enroll.
Concentration: Law and Social Structure, Law and Social Change, Global and Comparative Law
Description: The Law and Society major provides an interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary liberal arts approach to the study of law and legal institutions, and their impact on society. In this major, law is studied as a social institution, in the context of both the humanities and the social sciences. Students are encouraged to develop a critical understanding of legal institutions, and of law in its social, cultural, and historical contexts. Law and Society majors take a core set of courses offered by the Sociology Department, and then select courses from Sociology and from several other departments in the College of Arts and Sciences, and from the Wharton School. Students are introduced to the various modes of inquiry used in legal studies, including historical, philosophical, and social science approaches.

Requirements: Application requirements are for admission to the undergraduate College of Arts & Sciences. Required documents include the Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Essay, an official high school transcript, a school report, one counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, a mid-year report, and a final report. An application fee or fee waiver is also required. Standardized tests like the SAT or ACT are optional for the 2024-25 application cycle.
Concentration: ['Concentration in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies (ASLD)', 'General Linguistics Concentration', 'Concentration in Language and Cognition', 'Concentration in Language and Social Structure', 'Concentration in Language and the Brain']
Description: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. It is a multifaceted discipline that addresses the structure of language (phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics) as well as the social and cultural aspects of language (sociolinguistics, historical linguistics), how language is acquired (language acquisition), and how it is represented in the mind (psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics). A major in linguistics offers an excellent basis for a variety of careers in fields such as education, computer science, psychology, law, and many other fields.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Logic, Information, & Computation,
Requirements: Application requirements are not specific to the Logic, Information, & Computation major but are for admission to the undergraduate school (the College of Arts and Sciences). First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required components include the Penn-specific Essay, an official high school transcript, a School Report, a mid-year report, a final report, and three letters of recommendation (one from a counselor and two from teachers).
Concentration: ['Cognitive Science (LGIC-COGS)', 'Computation and Logic (LGIC-COMP)', 'Logic and Language (LGIC-LANG)', 'Mathematical Logic (LGIC-MATH)']
Description: The Logic, Information, and Computation (LGIC) major, administered by the Department of Mathematics, is an interdisciplinary major that provides students with a strong foundation in the core principles of logic, computation, and information, especially as they are applied in mathematics, computer science, linguistics, and philosophy. The LGIC major is designed to appeal to students with a variety of interests, since the major allows students to choose one of four concentrations: Cognitive Science (LGIC-COGS), Computation and Logic (LGIC-COMP), Logic and Language (LGIC-LANG), and Mathematical Logic (LGIC-MATH).

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Mathematical Economics,
Description: The Mathematical Economics major is an interdepartmental major between the Economics Department (in the School of Arts and Sciences) and the Statistics and Data Science Department (in the Wharton School). The major is very challenging and is suitable only for those students with a strong interest in and an aptitude for mathematics. The major seeks to endow the student with the basic tools of the professional economist. It provides an excellent background for graduate study in economics. Mathematical Economics is a major in the College of Arts and Sciences. It does not lead to a degree from the Wharton School.

Requirements: Prospective students must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. Required application components include the Penn-specific Essay, an Official High School Transcript, a School Report, one Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. A Mid-Year Report is required when first-term senior grades are available, and a Final Report is required for admitted students who choose to enroll. Standardized test scores (ACT or SAT) are optional for the 2024-25 admissions cycle.
Concentration: ['Applied Mathematics and Computational Science Concentration', 'Mathematical Biology Concentration']
Description: The major in Mathematics is intended for students who are interested in mathematics and its applications. It is also for those who plan to pursue graduate work in mathematics, or in such related fields as statistics, operations research, computer science, economics, finance, or business. For those interested primarily in applications or in the teaching of mathematics, it is possible to specialize in those areas. Flexibility is the keynote of the mathematics major. Please see the Mathematics Department website for more information.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Middle Eastern Languages & Cultures,
Requirements: Prospective students apply to the University of Pennsylvania's undergraduate program, typically through the College of Arts & Sciences, and declare their major after matriculating. The application requirements are for general first-year admission and include: Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report (due after first-term senior year grades are available), and Final Report (for admitted students who choose to enroll). Standardized testing (SAT/ACT) is optional for the 2024-25 application cycle.
Description: The major in Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures is designed for students who seek a linguistically-grounded and interdisciplinary approach to the study of the Middle East. The major builds upon the language and culture foundation of the area of the student's primary language of study. Students will choose one of the five languages taught in the department as a focus language: Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi/Urdu, Persian, or Turkish. Students will take two advanced language courses beyond the language requirement, and a total of ten courses that count toward the major. Majors are required to take NELC 0100 Introduction to the Middle East, as well as a senior research seminar, NELC 3000, in which they will produce a capstone research paper. The remaining six courses will consist of departmentally-approved courses, three of which must be at the 2000-level or higher.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Modern Middle Eastern Studies,
Requirements: Prospective undergraduate students apply to a specific undergraduate school at the University of Pennsylvania, not to a major. The application is submitted via the Common Application or Coalition Application. General requirements include: the application form, a Penn-specific essay, official high school transcript, a school report, letters of recommendation (from a counselor and two teachers), a mid-year report, and a final report for matriculating students. There are no specific requirements listed for admission directly into the Modern Middle Eastern Studies major.
Concentration: Anthropology and Sociology of the Middle East, History of the Middle East, Islamic Studies, Politics of the Middle East
Description: The major in Modern Middle Eastern Studies (MMES) offers a course of study for students interested in the politics, history, religion, languages, and cultures of the region. This interdisciplinary major provides an opportunity for students to study the Middle East using the methodologies of various departments, including Anthropology, History, History of Art, Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Political Science, and Religious Studies. Majors receive thorough grounding in the history and politics of the modern Middle East, gain proficiency in a Middle Eastern language, and take a sequence of courses organized around one of four distinct concentrations: Anthropology and Sociology, History, Islamic Studies, and Politics. The major is designed to provide a sound liberal arts background for students interested in pursuing graduate studies or in careers in which a knowledge of the Middle East is essential, such as diplomacy, government, journalism, and business.

Concentration: ['Musicology', 'Ethnomusicology', 'Theory', 'Composition', 'Performance', 'Jazz and Popular Music', 'Music Technology']
Description: The Music major at Penn is designed to allow students to explore music from a variety of perspectives. The curriculum develops students' musicianship skills while offering a background in a variety of musical traditions and repertoires. Students majoring in music explore the cultural and historical contexts of music, as well as the theoretical and compositional techniques that underlie musical works. Music majors gain a strong background in music while also receiving a broad liberal arts education. This prepares them for graduate study in music, as well as for careers in many fields, including arts administration, business, education, law, medicine, music criticism and journalism, and performance, as well as other related areas.

Neuroscience is an interdisciplinary major that provides a strong background for students interested in the biological bases of thought and behavior. The curriculum is intended for students who wish to pursue graduate work in neuroscience, medicine, or related fields, and to provide the appropriate science background for other professions such as law, business, and education. Required courses are drawn from biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, and psychology.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Nutrition Science,
Description: Nutrition science is the study of how food affects the body. It covers a wide range of topics, from the biochemical processes involved in metabolism to the social and behavioral factors that influence food choices. The Nutrition Science major at Penn is a basic science-based curriculum that prepares students for careers in medicine and other health professions, biomedical research, and public health. All students in the Nutrition Science major must complete the pre-med requirements. Our graduates are competitive candidates for medical, dental, and other health professional schools. Graduates of the program are also well prepared for graduate study leading to research, and for positions in industry, government, and other institutions that require a strong science background. All students in the Nutrition Science major take courses in chemistry, biology, physics, and math to establish a solid foundation in the basic sciences. Students in the major also take a sequence of three nutrition courses, including NUTR 1000 Nutrition and the Consumer, NUTR 2000 Nutrition and Metabolism, and NUTR 3300 Nutrition and the Life Cycle. Through these courses, students will gain an understanding of the functions of nutrients, the metabolic and physiologic consequences of nutrient deficiencies and excesses in human populations, and the role of nutrition in health and disease.

Requirements: The following is a list of items you’ll need to complete your application: Common Application or Coalition Application, Powered by Scoir; Penn-specific Essay; $75 application fee or fee waiver; Official high school transcript; School Report; Counselor Recommendation; Two Teacher Recommendations; Mid-Year Report (due when first-term senior grades are available); Final Report (due for matriculating students only).
Concentration: Philosophy and Science (PASC)
Description: The major in philosophy is designed to acquaint students with the fundamentals of philosophical reasoning and to provide them with a sophisticated understanding of the major figures and periods in the history of philosophy, as well as the central problems and areas of the discipline in the present day. Through their coursework, students will develop and hone their abilities to think and write with clarity, rigor, and intellectual imagination. The Department encourages its majors to pursue a broad liberal arts education, and many of our students double-major in a variety of other fields. For those who choose to continue their philosophical studies in graduate school, we offer a rich and demanding curriculum; however, the philosophy major also provides an excellent preparation for many other professions, including law, medicine, business, and public service.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy, Politics and Economics,
Concentration: Choice, Behavior and Markets, Constitutionalism and Governance, Distributive Justice, Globalization, Public Policy and a Fourth Course
Description: The Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) major has a long and distinguished history. It was born at Oxford University in the 1920s out of the conviction that study of the great modern works of social, political, and economic thought would be a good preparation for students entering the civil service and public life. It has since become a highly successful and influential program of study around the world. The PPE major at Penn provides a multidisciplinary education to students who want to become leaders in public affairs and in the national and international business communities. The major rests on the view that an understanding of the contemporary world requires knowledge of the principles of economic and political science, informed by the rigor of philosophical thought.

Requirements: To apply for first-year admission to the University of Pennsylvania, applicants must submit the Common Application or Coalition Application, which includes a personal essay, along with a Penn-specific Essay. Additional required documents include a $75 application fee or fee waiver, official high school transcript, School Report, a Counselor Recommendation, and two Teacher Recommendations. Applicants must also submit a Mid-Year Report and a Final Report upon availability. For the 2024-25 admissions cycle, applicants are required to submit either SAT or ACT scores.
Description: The Physics B.A. is a more flexible program for students who may be interested in a career in medicine, law, business, education, or other fields. Although the B.A. degree may be sufficient to qualify students for some positions in industry or government, it is not usually considered adequate preparation for doctoral study in physics. It can, however, provide an excellent background for graduate work in other sciences.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Political Science,
Requirements: To apply as a first-year student, applicants must submit either the Common Application or the Coalition Application. The application includes a personal essay and a Penn-specific essay. Required supporting documents include an official high school transcript, a school report, one counselor recommendation, and two teacher recommendations. A Mid-Year Report with first semester/trimester senior grades is also required. Standardized test scores (SAT or ACT) are optional. An alumni interview is also part of the application process.
Concentration: ['American Politics (AP)', 'Comparative Politics (CP)', 'International Relations (IR)', 'Political Theory (PT)', 'Public Policy and Governance (PPG)', 'Race, Ethnicity and Politics (REP)']
Description: The Undergraduate Program in Political Science is one of the largest undergraduate majors in the School of Arts and Sciences. It is also one of the most distinguished. Its faculty have international reputations, are leaders in their respective fields, and have been recognized both by the American Political Science Association and the University of Pennsylvania for their distinguished research and their teaching excellence. Our goal is to provide students with a deep and comprehensive understanding of politics. Politics is the process through which societies make collective decisions and determine how to distribute power and resources. The study of politics at Penn therefore encompasses a very broad range of topics, including: the meaning of democracy, the nature of personal liberty, the causes of war and peace, the sources of political and economic development, the challenges of environmental protection, the role of international organizations, the determinants of election outcomes, the nature of public opinion, and the meaning of justice and equality. To address these and other important questions, we offer an array of courses organized around four broad subfields of Political Science: American Politics, Comparative Politics, International Relations, and Political Theory.

Concentration: Cognitive Neuroscience, Clinical & Positive Psychology, Social & Personality Psychology
Description: Psychology is a science devoted to understanding human behavior, and the major at Penn is designed to give students an understanding of the important questions, methodologies, and findings in the major areas of this diverse field. Core course requirements ensure that students are exposed to the social, cognitive, developmental, and biological bases of behavior, and develop skills in the research methods and statistical techniques that are used to advance our understanding of these topics. Advanced coursework allows students to explore areas of personal interest in greater depth. Students are also encouraged to get involved in the research of the department by taking independent study courses with faculty members, or through paid research assistantships.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Religious Studies,
Requirements: Application requirements are for undergraduate admission to the College of Arts and Sciences, not specifically for the Religious Studies major. General requirements include: The Common Application or Coalition Application, a Penn-specific Supplement, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, Two Teacher Recommendations, Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report upon matriculation.
Description: What is religion? How can we best study it? The major and minor in Religious Studies provide students with the opportunity to explore the variety of religious traditions, and to learn different methods and approaches to understanding them. The Religious Studies curriculum reflects a wide spectrum of historical and cultural traditions, ranging from the ancient Near East to modern America, from the Abrahamic faiths of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam to the religions of Asia and Africa. The curriculum also introduces majors and minors to a variety of theories and methods to study those religious traditions. In the major, each student works with a faculty advisor to develop a course of study that reflects the student's own particular interests, while also meeting the requirements of the major. The major thus offers a well-defined structure, but also considerable flexibility. As they take a range of courses in the department, students become acquainted with religious phenomena and learn about various scholarly approaches to the academic study of religion (e.g., historical, anthropological, sociological, philosophical, literary, etc.). Religious Studies majors and minors develop the ability to read analytically, think critically, and write cogently. They also gain the specific skills to apply these abilities to the cross-cultural study of religion in its historical context, as well as the contemporary role of religion in global affairs.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Russian and East European Studies,
Concentration: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; Russian and East European Studies
Description: The major in Russian and East European Studies offers a choice of two concentrations: Russian Language, Literature, and Culture; and Russian and East European Studies. The major in REES is designed to provide B.A. candidates with a broad, interdisciplinary background in the languages, literatures, cultures, and histories of Russia and Eastern Europe, and a more specific focus for those who intend to go on to an M.A. or Ph.D. program in these fields. Students who complete the major requirements will acquire significant reading and speaking ability in one or two of the region's languages; a sophisticated understanding of the historical, cultural, and social forces that have shaped Russia and Eastern Europe; and the research, analytical, and writing skills that are necessary for advanced work in the humanities and social sciences. Students are strongly encouraged to study abroad in Russia or Eastern Europe for at least one semester or a summer. The Russian and East European Studies Program is an undergraduate component of the Department of Russian and East European Studies. The department's program in Russian and East European Studies is recognized as a National Resource Center by the US Department of Education.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Science, Technology and Society,
Description: Science, Technology, and Society (STSC) is a liberal arts major that focuses on one of the most important forces in modern life. The major prepares students to understand and participate in a world that is profoundly shaped by science and technology. It provides a strong foundation for citizenship, for careers in law, business, and public policy, as well as for graduate study in the humanities and social sciences. STSC courses analyze the historical, social, political, economic, and cultural dimensions of science, technology, and medicine. Some courses focus on the development of particular sciences or technologies, while others examine specific ethical or policy issues, such as those related to the internet, to health care, or to the environment. All students in the major learn how different disciplines in the humanities and social sciences study science and technology.

Requirements: First-year applicants must submit either the Common Application or Coalition Application. Required documents include: a Penn-specific Essay, Official High School Transcript, School Report, Counselor Recommendation, two Teacher Recommendations, a Mid-Year Report, and a Final Report. For Early Decision applicants, an Early Decision Agreement is also required.
Concentration: Cities, Communities, and Regions; Global, Transnational, and Comparative Sociology; Law and Society; Quantitative Methods; Sociology of Culture
Description: Sociology is the study of the social lives of people, groups, and societies. It addresses the most challenging issues of our time, from the social causes and consequences of racism, poverty, crime, and environmental degradation to the social dynamics of business, technology, social media, and social movements. Sociology examines how social structures, institutions, and cultures are created and how they affect human action and social change. Sociology provides a unique understanding of how societies function and what can be done to address social problems.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in South Asia Studies,
Description: The undergraduate major in South Asia Studies provides an excellent framework for understanding the history, cultures, and societies of this vast, diverse, and important part of the world. South Asia—which encompasses Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka—is home to roughly one-quarter of the world’s population, two of the world’s major religions (Hinduism and Buddhism), one of the world’s largest Muslim populations, and a fascinating array of languages and cultural traditions. The major is broadly interdisciplinary, offering students the opportunity to explore this region from a wide variety of perspectives, including anthropology, archaeology, art history, cinema and media studies, history, history of art, literary and cultural studies, music, political science, religious studies, and sociology. As a part of the major, students are expected to gain proficiency in a South Asian language. The South Asia Studies major prepares students for graduate study as well as a range of professional careers, including education, government, international business, journalism, law, medicine, and non-profit/non-governmental organization (NGO) work.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Theatre Arts,
Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Concentration: Performance Concentration, Theatre and Performance Studies Concentration
Description: The Theatre Arts major offers a unique opportunity for students to combine a rigorous, writing-intensive academic course of study with a diverse and challenging artistic practice. The major combines the study of dramatic literature, theatre history, performance theory and criticism, and performance practice within a liberal arts context. Courses embrace a broad spectrum of cross-cultural and interdisciplinary methods, and the faculty brings a wide range of expertise and artistic experience to the program. The major also provides opportunities for students to pursue intensive, pre-professional training in performance, design, and playwriting. Majors participate in an annual season of performances and events through the Theatre Arts Program and Penn Players Student Theatre, and are encouraged to take advantage of the numerous professional theatres located in Philadelphia. Courses in theatre provide credit towards the B.A. degree and are designed to develop students' critical and creative abilities and to expand their understanding of the relationship between theatre and society. Students graduating with a Theatre Arts major have successfully pursued advanced degrees at leading academic and professional training programs, as well as careers in the performing arts, film and television, arts management, casting, dramaturgy, law, education, business, and medicine. The Theatre Arts Program also offers a Minor in Theatre Arts and a Minor in Performance and is a partner in the Music Theatre Minor. Information on all three minors is available on the Theatre Arts website and elsewhere in the Catalog. The Theatre Arts Program is part of a collaborative relationship between the University of Pennsylvania and the Pig Iron Theatre Company, a partnership that supports professional training in devised performance. The Theatre Arts Program also engages in collaborative artistic and academic programming with a number of arts and culture organizations across campus.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Urban Studies,
Requirements: Application to an undergraduate program like Urban Studies, BA is done through the general first-year application process. The required components are: The Common Application or Coalition Application, Penn-specific essays, a $75 application fee or fee waiver, official high school transcript, School Report, one counselor recommendation, two teacher recommendations, and a Mid-Year Report. A Final Report is required in June from admitted students who choose to enroll. Standardized tests (SAT/ACT) are optional.
Concentration: Cities and Society; Urban Development and Commerce
Description: The Urban Studies Program at the University of Pennsylvania offers a liberal arts-based, interdisciplinary approach to the study of urban life. The program draws on the social sciences and humanities, as well as the professional schools, to provide students with a broad-based understanding of cities and urban systems. A major in Urban Studies consists of twelve courses. Of these, six are the Urban Studies "core curriculum." The remaining six courses are an area of concentration that the student creates in conjunction with the Urban Studies academic advisor. The Urban Studies major has two concentrations: Cities and Society; and Urban Development and Commerce.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Visual Studies,
Description: Visual Studies is an interdisciplinary undergraduate major in the College of Arts and Sciences that focuses on vision and visuality in the arts, humanities, and social, and natural sciences. The major consists of a variety of courses that are designed to develop visual literacy and critical seeing.

Requirements: The Africana Studies minor is a six-course program of study. At least four of the courses for the minor must be taken at the University of Pennsylvania. In order to receive credit for the minor, a student must receive a grade of C or better in all courses for the minor. Students interested in the minor should consult the Undergraduate Chair.
Description: The Africana Studies minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to the study of the history, culture and social-political realities of Africans and people of African descent throughout the world. The curriculum seeks to provide students with a deep and broad understanding of the links between the social, economic, political and cultural dimensions of the Africana experience, including the creative expression of these experiences in literature, music, art and dance. The curriculum, therefore, highlights both the historical and contemporary experiences of Africans and their descendants in Africa, the U.S., the Caribbean and Latin America.

Requirements:
The minor in American Public Policy (APPC) requires six courses for a total of six course units.
1. One introductory course on American politics or public policy.
2. One course in statistics.
3. Four elective courses, with at least two at the 2000-level or above.
Concentration: Law and Social Policy, Education Policy, Environmental Policy, Health Policy, Urban Policy and Community Development, Race and Ethnic Policy
Description: The American Public Policy (APPC) minor focuses on the American political process and the analysis of U.S. public policy. It is designed to provide students with the analytic tools necessary for an understanding of the politics and economics of public policy and with in-depth exposure to at least one substantive policy area. Students will develop an understanding of how issues get on the political agenda, how political institutions and processes shape policy choices, and how the consequences of policy are evaluated. They will also gain an understanding of the economic justification for government intervention in the economy, and the potential for government failure. The minor requires a single course in statistics, one introductory course in either microeconomics or American politics, three courses from a list of core courses in public policy analysis and processes, and two courses in a substantive policy area such as education policy, health care policy, environmental policy, or urban policy.

ProgramName: American Sign Language and Deaf Studies Minor
Description: The minor in American Sign Language and Deaf Studies, housed in the Department of Linguistics, consists of six course units. The minor gives students a comprehensive introduction to the language and culture of the Deaf community in the United States. Four courses are in the acquisition of American Sign Language (ASL), and two are in Deaf studies. These two courses are taught in English and have no pre-requisites.

Requirements:
A total of 6 course units are required.

Two courses in Ancient History (ANCH) at any level
Four additional course units chosen from the list below in at least two of the following categories:
Ancient History
Classical Civilization
Greek
Latin
Approved related fields
Description: Ancient history is an interdisciplinary field that draws on literary and material evidence to study the ancient Mediterranean world, from the second millennium BCE to (in some areas) the eighth century CE. It embraces a wide variety of cultures and regions, from Mesopotamia and the Near East through Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to the western provinces of the Roman empire. At Penn, ancient history is an interdepartmental major and minor jointly sponsored by the Departments of Classical Studies and History and administered through the Graduate Group in Ancient History.

Requirements: The Archeological Science Minor requires a minimum of 6 course units. To declare a minor, contact the undergraduate chair.
Description: The undergraduate minor in Archaeological Science provides students with a strong background in the scientific analysis of archaeological materials. Students will be exposed to the major methods used in archaeological science and will learn to interpret scientific data derived from archaeological finds in a theoretically-informed manner. Coursework introduces students to the major analytical tools available for scientific analysis of ancient artifacts and ecofacts, while required laboratory or field experience provides direct exposure to the practice of archaeological science. In consultation with the minor advisor, students may specialize in one of three major areas: archaeobotany (the analysis of ancient plant remains), zooarchaeology (the study of ancient animal remains), or the analysis of archaeological artifacts.

Department: School of Arts and Sciences, Stuart Weitzman School of Design
Description: The Architectural History Minor is designed for students who want a broad-based introduction to the history of architecture, landscape architecture, and urbanism. The minor allows students to explore these histories from multiple disciplinary perspectives and to learn how to research and write about the built environment. It provides an especially strong basis for students interested in further graduate study in architectural history and theory, art history, historic preservation, and landscape studies.

The undergraduate minor in Architecture provides a broad introductory survey of the field of architecture in the context of a liberal arts education. It fosters an understanding of architecture as a cultural practice, a technological craft, and a profession. The program is designed for students who wish to gain a critical understanding of architecture and urbanism. The architecture minor also serves as an introduction for those students who plan to continue their education in architecture on a graduate level.

Requirements: In order to declare the minor, students must fill out the Declare/Update Field of Study Form on Path@Penn and meet with the Program Manager.
Description: The Asian American Studies (ASAM) undergraduate minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to understanding the histories, communities, and contemporary experiences of Asians in the Americas. The program highlights the creative and intellectual productions of Asian Americans, as well as their social and political struggles. Students are encouraged to develop a comparative and critical perspective on Asian American experiences by taking courses in other ethnic studies programs, as well as by taking courses that place Asian Americans in a global and diasporic context. Through a broad range of courses in ethnic studies, the humanities and the social sciences, the minor in Asian American studies provides a strong foundation for students interested in a variety of fields and careers, including law, medicine and public health, social work, education, journalism, public policy, and arts and culture.

The undergraduate minor in Bioethics, offered through the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at the Perelman School of Medicine, provides an opportunity for students to systematically study the ethical, legal, and social implications of advances in biomedicine and the life sciences. The minor requires six courses in bioethics. Course offerings range from the introductory "What is Bioethics?" to more advanced seminars on topics including clinical ethics, research ethics, neuroethics, law and ethics, and global health ethics. Students have the opportunity to count courses from departments and schools across the University. The Bioethics Minor is open to all undergraduate students at the University of Pennsylvania.

Requirements: To declare a minor, students should meet with the undergraduate chair or program advisor in the sponsoring department to discuss their interests and plan a course of study. A Minor Declaration Form must be completed, signed by the minor advisor, and returned to the College Office.

Description: The undergraduate minor in biophysics is aimed at students with interests at the interface of physical and life sciences. The curriculum consists of a combination of core and elective courses in biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics, chosen to provide the breadth and depth required for this interdisciplinary field. The program is designed both for students who have a strong interest in biophysics but major in another subject, and for students who decide to major in biophysics late in their careers. It gives formal recognition to students who have made a serious commitment to biophysics.

Requirements: Students may satisfy the requirements for a Minor in Chemistry by completing six (6) course units in Chemistry as listed below. Four (4) of the six (6) courses must be numbered 200 or above. The courses used to fulfill the minor must be taken for a letter grade, not pass/fail. Lab courses cannot be counted toward the minor. Research courses may not be used to satisfy the requirements for the minor.
Description: The Chemistry Minor will provide students a strong background in the core aspects of chemistry, which could include organic, inorganic, physical, biological and materials chemistry. Chemistry is the central science and it provides the fundamental basis to understand biological processes, materials science, earth science and many other fields. This minor could serve as an excellent complement for majors in biology, physics, engineering, earth science, nursing or other majors in which a strong chemistry background will be beneficial for a future career.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The undergraduate minor in Cinema and Media Studies offers a structured, interdisciplinary curriculum, which is organized to provide a solid grounding in the history, theory, and aesthetics of film and media. The minor is offered to all undergraduate students in the College of Arts and Sciences, Wharton, Engineering, and Nursing.

Requirements: The minor in Classical Studies consists of any six course units from the offerings of the Department of Classical Studies. A student may elect a general minor in Classical Studies or may concentrate in Greek, Latin, Ancient History, or Classical Civilization. The course requirements for the minors in Greek, Latin, Ancient History, and Classical Civilization are six courses from the respective subfield, as approved by the undergraduate chair. The requirements for the General Classical Studies minor are any six CLST courses, at least three of which must be at the 2000-level or higher. No more than one course may be at the 1000-level.
Description: The minor in Classical Studies is designed for students who want to become broadly familiar with the discipline of Classical Studies but do not have the time to devote to a full major. A student may minor in Classical Studies by taking any six courses in the department (CLST, GREK or LATN).

Cognitive science is the study of the human mind and its processes. An interdisciplinary field, it draws on many fields including psychology, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, and neuroscience. Students learn about the mind from many different levels, ranging from high-level tasks like reasoning and decision-making, to the neural mechanisms that subserve them. Research experience is an important part of the major, and students are strongly encouraged to work in a lab, whether it is for independent study course credit or on a volunteer basis. For more information please see the Cognitive Science Program website.
ScholarshipType: Need-based grants, Named Scholarships, Federal grants, State grants. A small number of merit-based music and ROTC scholarships are also available.

Description: Comparative Literature is the study of literature and culture across linguistic, national and disciplinary boundaries. The program teaches students to think critically and write cogently about a wide variety of texts, from ancient philosophy to contemporary film. Courses are cross-listed in a wide variety of departments in the humanities and social sciences. The program provides an excellent foundation for graduate study in literature, theory, and cultural studies, as well as for professional training in law, journalism, publishing, and other fields.

The minor in Computational Neuroscience (CN) is designed for students interested in the computational principles that govern how we think, perceive, and act. The minor integrates a diverse, interdisciplinary set of courses from contributing departments including Biology (BIOL), Bioengineering (BE), Computer and Information Science (CIS), Electrical and Systems Engineering (ESE), Linguistics (LING), Mathematics (MATH), Philosophy (PHIL), Physics (PHYS), and Psychology (PSYC). Students will learn to use mathematical and computational tools to understand brain function and to probe the relationship between the brain and behavior. This minor will be especially attractive to students who have an interest in quantitative and computational approaches to studying the mind and brain, regardless of their major.

Requirements: The Consumer Psychology Minor is a six-course, cross-school minor for students in the College of Arts and Sciences. Students in the College may declare the minor at any time by meeting with an advisor in the Psychology undergraduate office and listing it on their worksheet in Path@Penn.
Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The Consumer Psychology Minor, offered by the School of Arts and Sciences and the Wharton School, is an interdisciplinary program that focuses on the psychological aspects of marketing and consumer behavior. Students who graduate with this minor will have a strong foundation for pursuing graduate studies or a career in marketing. The minor requires a total of 6 course units.

The Creative Writing Minor offers undergraduate students the opportunity to specialize in the writing of fiction, poetry, nonfiction, screenwriting, playwriting, and journalism. Through a series of workshops and seminars, students develop and hone their literary talents and creative skills. To complete the minor, students must take six courses from the Creative Writing Program's offerings, including at least three writing workshops. A maximum of one course may be taken in a related discipline, with the prior approval of the Creative Writing Program Director.

Requirements: The minor is open to all undergraduate students in the College. Interested students should consult with the program co-directors to discuss their interests and course of study. A declaration form must be completed and signed by the student and one of the program co-directors.
Description: The Data Science & Analytics Minor is designed for students who want to develop a strong understanding of the principles and methods of data science and learn how to apply them to their own major fields of study. The minor will provide students with the foundational skills to collect, analyze, and interpret data, and to communicate their findings effectively. The minor is a joint program between the College of Arts and Sciences and the Wharton School, and is open to students from both schools.

Requirements: The Digital Humanities minor is open to all undergraduate students at the University of Pennsylvania. To apply, students must fill out a short application form, which includes a brief statement of interest describing why they are interested in the minor and what they hope to learn.
Description: The Digital Humanities Minor provides students with an introduction to the key questions, methods, and skills involved in the emerging field of digital humanities. It allows students to bring the analytical and conceptual tools of their home disciplines to bear on digital materials, and also to bring digital tools to bear on the objects of traditional humanities and social-scientific inquiry. The minor is highly interdisciplinary, and is open to students in all undergraduate schools at Penn. It offers students opportunities both for critical reflection on the digital and hands-on engagement with new technologies.

The East Asian Area Studies (EAAS) undergraduate program provides students with a comprehensive, interdisciplinary education in the humanities and social sciences focused on East Asia. This program combines the study of East Asian languages (Chinese, Japanese, and Korean) with a wide array of disciplinary and interdisciplinary courses. Students may major or minor in EAAS.
The EAAS undergraduate program prepares students for graduate study and for professional careers in many fields, including business, law, government, international relations, and cultural and educational institutions.

ProgramName: East Asian Languages and Civilizations Minor
Requirements: The minor in East Asian Languages and Civilizations requires 6 course units. To declare a minor in EALC, please contact the EALC Undergraduate Chair.
Description:
The East Asian Languages and Civilizations Minor enables students to focus on a particular country or region of East Asia—China, Japan, or Korea—and its language and culture.

The minor consists of 6 course units chosen in consultation with the Undergraduate Chair. Four of these must be language courses in Chinese, Japanese, or Korean, at or above the 2000-level/second year. The remaining two courses must be non-language EALC courses focused on the same country/region as the language courses. The two non-language courses must be at the 2000-level or above. First-year seminars may be counted toward this requirement with the approval of the Undergraduate Chair. Language courses taken at the 1000-level may not be counted for the minor.

The Minor in East Central European Studies (ECES) is designed to provide students with a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of the lands and peoples between Germany and Russia. It focuses on the countries which since 1989 have experienced the most successful transition from communism to democratic free-market societies. These include Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Hungary, but also the Baltic states, other Balkan countries, and Ukraine. Courses are offered in the social sciences and humanities by an interdisciplinary group of faculty who meet regularly in a faculty seminar.

The minor in Economic Policy is intended for students with an interest in public policy who wish to supplement their major with an understanding of economic analysis and its applications. The curriculum emphasizes the connection between economic principles and policy applications. The core of the minor is built around four required courses. Microeconomic theory is a prerequisite. Students choose two additional courses from an approved list of electives. The minor is administered by the Department of Economics in the School of Arts and Sciences.

The undergraduate minor in Economics is designed to provide students with a rigorous, broad, and critical understanding of the methods and ideas of modern economics. The minor will require students to complete the core intermediate-level theory courses (ECON 101 and ECON 102) and one course in econometrics (ECON 103). Students will then be able to choose two additional economics courses from a broad range of electives that reflect the great variety of questions that modern economics addresses. Some of the many areas in which economics minors may take courses are law and economics, development economics, finance, industrial organization, international economics, labor economics, and public economics. The minor is flexible enough to fit a wide range of interests and goals.

The English minor consists of six courses in English, all of which must be taken at Penn. A grade of C or better is required for a course to be counted towards the minor. No more than one creative writing workshop may be counted towards the minor. AP credit does not count towards the minor. Up to two courses taken abroad with an approved study abroad program may be counted toward the minor, with the approval of the Undergraduate Chair.

Requirements: Students wishing to minor in Environmental Humanities should consult the ENVS Undergraduate Coordinator.
Description: The undergraduate minor in Environmental Humanities (EHM) provides a coherent, interdisciplinary course of study for students interested in the relationship between the environment and human culture. This flexible minor gives students opportunities to delve into key concepts, including nature, culture, environment, and ecology, and to ask fundamental questions about the human place in the world. Courses in the minor address such questions through the lens of history, literature, philosophy, religion, anthropology, and the arts, while building an understanding of how these fields engage with the natural, social, and health sciences. Students pursuing the minor complete six courses, including one designated introductory course, four approved electives, and one capstone seminar. The EHM minor is excellent preparation for careers in environmental law and public policy, journalism, arts, and education.

Requirements: Six course units are required. The coursework for the minor is intended to be flexible, but must include two introductory courses from different fields of environmental science, and four upper-level courses.
Description: The Environmental Science Minor provides a structured introduction to the scientific principles that are the foundation of understanding environmental issues. The curriculum provides a strong scientific background that prepares students to understand and address contemporary environmental challenges that often span multiple disciplines. The minor requires a core set of courses that provide an overview of environmental science, an introduction to key principles in geology, ecology, and chemistry, and a statistics course. Students must then complete three environmental science elective courses. Students are encouraged to pursue a cohesive theme in their electives, such as conservation, ecology, environmental chemistry, geology, marine science, or toxicology.

Requirements: To declare an ENVS minor, you need to set up a meeting with the undergraduate coordinator. To prepare for the meeting, students should review the course requirements and complete the Minor Declaration Form and the Minor Worksheet. The minor requires the completion of six course units.
Concentration: Sustainability and Environmental Management, Environmental Science, Environmental Humanities
Description:
The minor in Environmental Studies (ENVS) is designed for students who wish to gain a deeper understanding of the scientific, social, and humanistic dimensions of environmental issues. Courses in this program reflect the interdisciplinary nature of the field and provide a foundation in the study of natural and human systems and the interactions between them.

The ENVS minor is administered by the Department of Earth and Environmental Science. Students are encouraged to develop a specific course of study in consultation with the Environmental Studies Undergraduate Advisor.

To best prepare for a major or minor in Environmental Studies, students should plan to take the introductory course, ENVS 1000 Introduction to Environmental Studies, early in their career. Students interested in the ENVS minor should see the Environmental Studies Undergraduate Advisor as soon as possible.

The minor in European Studies is designed to encourage students to think broadly about Europe in a comparative, interdisciplinary way. It will allow students with an interest in Europe to extend their knowledge beyond a single discipline by taking courses in multiple departments and programs. Administered by the Department of Germanic Languages and Literatures, the minor draws from departments and programs across the School of Arts and Sciences. With the guidance of the undergraduate chair, students will design their own curriculum of 6 course units to explore an area or topic of interest.

The undergraduate minor in Fine Arts is designed for students who are interested in the practice of visual arts. The minor is made up of a structured set of studio art and art history courses, which encourage each student to focus on one of the following areas: drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, photography, video and animation. The Weitzman School of Design Department of Fine Arts & Design administers this minor and provides an advisor for the students.

The French and Francophone Studies minor consists of six courses chosen in consultation with the Undergraduate Chair. Students may design a minor that focuses on literature, cinema, or cultural studies, or one that has a broader interdisciplinary focus. All courses must be taught in French. At least four of the six courses must be taken at Penn.

ProgramName: Gender, Sexuality and Women's Studies Minor
Requirements: Students who wish to declare a major or a minor in Gender, Sexuality, and Women's Studies should meet with the Undergraduate Chair to plan a course of study. Please contact the Program Coordinator to make an appointment.
Description: The Gender, Sexuality, and Women's Studies Program offers an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides a critical, cross-cultural, and historical perspective on gender, sexuality, and women's issues. The Program provides students with the critical tools to analyze the construction and consequences of gender and sexuality categories in all areas of life, including the law, science, politics, the family, the workplace, art, and literature. Courses are offered by affiliated faculty from a wide variety of schools and departments including American Civilization, Anthropology, Art History, Cinema Studies, Communications, Comparative Literature, Criminology, East Asian Languages and Civilizations, Economics, English, Folklore, French, Germanic Languages and Literatures, Health and Societies, History, History and Sociology of Science, Legal Studies and Business Ethics, Music, Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Nursing, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Religious Studies, Romance Languages, Slavic Languages and Literatures, Social Policy and Practice, and Sociology. Students may take courses from any of these departments to complete their major. For course descriptions, please see the GSWS website. Please consult the GSWS Program with any questions regarding courses.

Requirements: The University of Pennsylvania refers to the program as the 'Earth Science Minor'. To declare the minor, students should meet with an EES (Earth and Environmental Science) undergraduate advisor to plan a course of study.
Description: The Geology minor requires 6 course units, as follows: EESC 2300, EESC 2400, or EESC 2500. Four additional courses, numbered EESC 2000 or higher. One course at any level.

The German minor consists of six courses. A student may receive credit for only one course in the GRMN 2000-2099 range. No more than two courses may be non-language courses. At least 3 CU must be taken at Penn. Students work with the undergraduate chair to design a course of study that best fits their interests. In addition to a wide range of courses offered by the department at the 2000- and 3000-levels, students may wish to take related courses in other departments such as History, History of Art, Jewish Studies, Music, Philosophy, and Political Science. Upon approval of the undergraduate chair, these courses may count towards the minor. Students should select an advisor from the undergraduate faculty. The department will also accept up to two transfer credits from study abroad programs per semester, with a limit of four CUs.

Requirements: Students interested in the minor should consult the Undergraduate Chair, Dr. Julia Verkholantsev. The Undergraduate Chair will work with each student to develop an individualized course of study. A minor in Global Medieval Studies is formally declared through the College Office.
Description: The Global Medieval Studies minor at Penn is an interdisciplinary program that draws on the expertise of faculty in a wide variety of departments and programs across the School of Arts and Sciences, as well as the professional schools and local institutions. The minor gives students the opportunity to learn about the major cultural and historical developments that took place across the globe during the thousand-year period from roughly 500 to 1500 CE. Students can focus on a particular region (Europe, the Middle East, East Asia), or on a particular theme or approach (manuscript studies, urbanism, literary history, etc.), but all students will gain a broad perspective on the medieval world and an understanding of the diversity of its cultures as well as the extent of its global interconnectedness.

The Hispanic Studies Minor consists of 6 course units. All courses must be taught in Spanish. A maximum of one course in translation can be approved by the Undergraduate Chair. Students may count a maximum of two courses taken abroad toward the minor. For courses to be accepted, they must be pre-approved by the Undergraduate Chair.

The study of history gives students a broad perspective on the human experience and develops the intellectual skills of critical thinking and cogent writing. Students of history learn to locate and evaluate primary sources, to assess and compare conflicting interpretations, to understand the complexity of causation, and to write analytical essays. An undergraduate education in history provides an excellent preparation for many careers, including law, journalism, business, public service, and education.

The Art History minor consists of six courses. In consultation with the undergraduate chair, students will devise a program that reflects their particular interests and provides a broad introduction to the history of art. At least four of the six courses must be taken at Penn.

The International Development minor provides students with the opportunity to take a diverse course of study centered around a common interest in understanding poverty, wealth, and inequality in the developing world. The minor is explicitly interdisciplinary and is organized thematically in order to allow students to construct a course of study that both reflects their own interests and exposes them to different methodological and theoretical approaches. Students will also fulfill the minor's fieldwork experience requirement, providing them with the opportunity to directly engage with the complex issues surrounding economic and social development within developing countries.

The International Relations Minor is intended for students who wish to supplement their major with a multidisciplinary approach to the study of international affairs. A total of 6 course units are required for the minor. Students must have a minimum GPA of 3.0 to be approved for the minor. At least 4 of the 6 course units must be taken at Penn.

The Italian Studies minor is designed for students who want to develop a strong command of the Italian language and to cultivate an in-depth knowledge of Italian literature and culture. It is an ideal course of study for students who have a general interest in Italian culture and for those who wish to complement their major with a strong background in Italian. The minor is a particularly valuable asset to students majoring in art history, classics, comparative literature, history, international relations, linguistics, music and political science.

The Jewish Studies Minor enables students to sample the offerings of the Jewish Studies Program and to design a course of study that reflects their own interests, whether they be in Jewish history, religion, literature, or culture. Students who complete the minor will have a basic understanding of the breadth of Jewish civilization and will also have studied one or more areas of Jewish Studies in-depth.

The Journalistic Writing minor, administered through the Center for Programs in Contemporary Writing (CPCW), is designed for students interested in developing the skills of a journalist: to report and write with accuracy and clarity, to find and incorporate sources, to work under deadline, and to tell a story in a way that is vivid and compelling. In courses offered through the CPCW, including the writing of fiction, poetry, nonfiction, and screenplays, as well as in courses focused specifically on journalistic writing, students will hone their abilities to convey information to a public audience through a variety of media. Students interested in the minor should seek the advice of the Director of Journalistic Writing, Dick Polman, who will help them select an appropriate sequence of courses.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The Landscape Studies Minor provides undergraduate students with a multi-disciplinary approach to the study of landscape. Students examine landscape as a textual, visual, and material practice. They engage with a range of methods and theories used in the analysis of landscape from the arts and sciences, including anthropology, archaeology, architecture, classics, fine arts, geology, history of art, historic preservation, and urban studies. The minor consists of six courses: a gateway seminar, LSTD 1640 Introduction to Landscape Studies; a methods course; and four electives.

ProgramName: Latin American and Latinx Studies Minor
Requirements:
Six course units are required for the minor.

1 course unit may be at the 1000-level (introductory).
At least 2 course units must be from LALS courses.
No more than 2 course units may be in any one department (other than LALS).
At least 3 course units must be at the 2000-level or above.
All courses must be approved by the Undergraduate Chair.
Description: The Latin American and Latinx Studies (LALS) Program offers an interdisciplinary minor designed to provide students with a multifaceted and nuanced understanding of Latin America, the Caribbean and people of Latin American descent in the United States and other parts of the world. Students in the minor focus on the histories, cultures, and contemporary socio-economic and political contexts of the region and its peoples. The program encourages a hemispheric and transnational framework, with a particular emphasis on the links that connect Latin America and the Caribbean to other regions of the world, especially Africa and North America. The LALS minor complements a wide variety of majors. It helps prepare students for careers in foreign service, law, government, business, journalism, social service, education, and research, among other professions.

Law is a crucial element of social, political and economic life, a feature of all human societies. The Law and Society minor is designed for students who wish to understand the nature of law, the problems to which law is addressed, and the role of law in society. The courses in the minor come from several departments in the arts and sciences, including anthropology, criminology, history, philosophy, political science, sociology and from the Wharton School. Students completing the minor will have an intellectually coherent, interdisciplinary introduction to the study of law and society.

The Legal Studies and History Minor is an interdisciplinary minor open to all undergraduate students in the College, Wharton, SEAS, and Nursing. This minor has been designed for students interested in the law from a liberal arts perspective. The minor allows students to explore the ways in which the law and legal institutions of the United States have developed and the ways in which they have reflected social, cultural, and political change over the course of American history. Students who are considering a legal career but who want to study law in an undergraduate, liberal arts context will find this minor particularly attractive. But the minor will be equally appropriate for any student interested in learning more about the role of the law in American history and society, whether or not that student is contemplating law school.

Requirements: To declare a minor in linguistics, students should go to Path at Penn and submit a 'Declare/Update Field of Study' request. This is an internal process for currently enrolled University of Pennsylvania students.
Description: The Linguistics minor is designed for students who are interested in the nature of human language. Minors take a total of 6 course units, including a foundational course in linguistic analysis and a selection of more advanced courses covering the core areas of the field (sound structure, sentence structure, and meaning) as well as a variety of subfields and applications. The minor provides an excellent complement to a variety of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.

The Logic, Information, and Computation (LGIC) program is an interdisciplinary minor program that provides a formal and critical approach to computation and its applications in the digital age. This program brings together faculty from Computer and Information Science, Linguistics, Mathematics and Philosophy to teach in an integrated curriculum. It is a supplement, not a substitute, for a major in one of the participating disciplines. The curriculum is intended to prepare students for graduate work and for a variety of careers.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The undergraduate minor in Mathematics is designed to give students a strong background in the fundamentals of theoretical mathematics. Students interested in the minor should consult the undergraduate chair as early as possible.

Requirements: The Medical Sociology minor is available to all undergraduate students in the College. To declare the minor, students should meet with the undergraduate advisor in the Sociology Department.
Description: The Medical Sociology minor provides an opportunity to examine the social context of health, illness, and medical care. The curriculum gives students a sociological perspective, which is becoming increasingly important for a broad range of professional fields, including medicine, public health, hospital administration, medical law, and health policy. Medical sociologists study the social causes and patterns of health and disease; the social behavior of health care personnel and their patients; the social functions of health organizations and institutions; and the social patterns of the utilization of health services.

The Modern Middle Eastern Studies (MMES) undergraduate minor is designed to provide students with a broad, multi-disciplinary understanding of the modern Middle East, a region understood as stretching from Morocco to Afghanistan and including the Arab world, Iran, Israel, and Turkey. The coursework for the minor exposes students to a variety of disciplines and methodologies, with an emphasis on the social sciences and humanities. While language study is not required for the minor, MMES minors are strongly encouraged to achieve proficiency in a Middle Eastern language, such as Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, or Turkish.

Requirements:
The Music Minor requires 6 course credits, as follows:
- Two courses in music theory (MUSC 1700 and MUSC 1710)
- One course in music history
- Three music electives (chosen from any MUSC course)
Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
Description: The Music Minor is designed for students with a serious interest in music who wish to combine it with another major field of study. Students minoring in music should consult with the Undergraduate Chair in Music to plan their course of study as early as possible. A minimum of 6 course units is required.

ProgramName: Native American and Indigenous Studies Minor
Description: The undergraduate minor in Native American and Indigenous Studies (NAIS) introduces students to the core concepts, questions, and methods of the interdisciplinary field of Native American and Indigenous studies. Students in the NAIS minor will gain an understanding of the diversity of Indigenous cultures, histories, and languages in the Americas; the history and ongoing legacies of colonialism in the Americas; Indigenous epistemologies, spiritual traditions, and cultural practices; Indigenous intellectual traditions, including Indigenous scholarship and Indigenous traditional knowledges; and the politics and legal status of Indigenous peoples in the United States and internationally. Students can tailor the minor to meet their interests by choosing to focus on specific topics, time periods, Indigenous cultures, and/or geographic areas. The NAIS minor prepares students to apply their knowledge in fields such as education, law, public history, health, medicine, business, and public policy, and to pursue graduate studies in a number of fields.

ProgramName: Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures Minor
Description: The minor in Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures (MELC) provides students with the opportunity to learn about the histories and cultures of the Middle East while gaining proficiency in one of its languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, or Turkish). The minor is particularly well suited for students with an interest in the history, politics, religions, and cultures of the region, including those planning a career in which knowledge of the Middle East would be an asset. Many MELC minors have successfully combined their expertise in the region with majors in political science, history, religious studies, international relations, and business.

Requirements: Students wishing to declare a minor in Neuroscience should complete the declaration form on the BBB website.
Description: The Neuroscience Minor provides an opportunity for students to learn about the brain and nervous system from an interdisciplinary perspective. The minor exposes students to a variety of topics and levels of analysis in the field of neuroscience and is complementary to a wide range of majors.

Department: College of Arts and Sciences, The Wharton School

Concentration: Basic Nutrition Science Track, Nutrition in the Life Cycle Track
Description: The Nutrition Science Minor, offered by the School of Nursing, provides students with a foundation in the science of nutrition and its application to health. The minor offers two tracks, the Basic Nutrition Science Track and the Nutrition in the Life Cycle Track, each of which provides an in-depth look at specific aspects of nutrition science. The minor will be of particular interest to students in the life sciences, as well as those planning careers in the health professions, but is open to all undergraduate students.

Requirements: To declare a minor in Philosophy, students must do so using Path@Penn. The declaration is then submitted to the department for approval.

The minor in physics consists of 8 course units: PHYS 0150/PHYS 0170, PHYS 0151/PHYS 0171, MATH 1400, MATH 1410, and MATH 2400, plus three additional physics courses, two of which must be at the 2000-level or higher. The requirements for the minor must be completed with a minimum GPA of 2.0. To declare a minor, students must submit a Declaration of Minor form.
Description: The Physics minor consists of 6 courses. Two course units are required from the introductory physics sequence. The PHYS 0150-PHYS 0151 sequence is recommended, especially for those students contemplating a major in the sciences or engineering. Four additional courses are chosen from PHYS 0200 and above, including at least two courses from PHYS 0300 and above. PHYS 0495 is not allowed for the minor.

Requirements: Students should fill out the Declare/Update Field of Study Form on Path@Penn to declare the minor. This form should be submitted no later than the "drop" period of the student's final semester. Students are encouraged to talk with the undergraduate coordinator or associate director to be sure they have fulfilled the requirements.

Description: The Psychoanalytic Studies Minor offers undergraduates the opportunity to pursue an interdisciplinary course of study that focuses on the theory, application, and history of psychoanalysis. From its origins in the clinical neurology of the nineteenth century, psychoanalysis has had a revolutionary and enduring impact across the humanities, arts, and social sciences. As a theory of the mind, a method of inquiry and interpretation, and a therapeutic practice, psychoanalysis has transformed modern and contemporary understandings of human subjectivity, meaning, and motivation. The minor introduces students to the foundational texts and concepts of psychoanalysis and then allows them to explore its influence across a wide range of disciplines, including history, literature, film, politics, and gender and sexuality studies. The minor also helps prepare students interested in pursuing clinical careers in psychology, social work, and medicine.

Requirements: The requirements for the Psychology minor are any 6 course units in Psychology.
Description: The Psychology Minor introduces students to the main areas of this discipline. A student minoring in psychology takes an introductory course (PSYC 0001), 2 courses from the foundational areas of the major (one from the Biological Science distribution and one from the Social Science distribution), and 3 additional courses of their choosing in Psychology. A minimum of 4 courses must be taken at Penn. A minimum of 4 courses must be taken in the Psychology Department. Students should speak to the Undergraduate Coordinator in Psychology to declare the minor.

The Religious Studies Minor offers students an opportunity to explore the vital role that religion plays in human societies. The minor is interdisciplinary. Our faculty have been trained in a variety of fields, including anthropology, history, sociology, textual studies, and philosophy, and our courses are cross-listed in a wide variety of departments. The minor offers a great deal of flexibility, enabling students to devise a program of study that is well-suited to their interests. The undergraduate chair is happy to assist students in this task.

ProgramName: Russian and East European Studies Minor
Requirements:
The Russian and East European Studies minor requires 6 course units, to be distributed as follows:

- 2 course units in Russian and East European language at the intermediate level or above, or demonstrated proficiency at the intermediate-mid level.
- 4 course units in Russia- and East Europe-related content courses from at least two departments. Up to 2 of these courses may be from language and literature courses at the intermediate level or above taught in the target language (beyond the 2 c.u. for the language requirement). A list of approved courses is maintained on the REES website.

At least three of the six courses for the minor must be taken at Penn.

Students must earn a grade of C or better in all courses for the minor.

Courses taken on a pass/fail basis cannot be counted toward the minor.
Description: The Russian and East European Studies (REES) major and minor introduce students to a strategically important and culturally rich region of the world: Russia, Ukraine, and other post-soviet states; Poland, the Czech and Slovak Republics, and other states of the former socialist bloc; and the diasporas of these countries.

The undergraduate minor in Science, Technology and Society (STSC) is designed to give students a sophisticated understanding of how science, technology and medicine are shaping our modern world. Courses in the minor focus on the social, cultural, political, economic and ethical dimensions of science, technology and medicine, in the past and in the present. The minor provides a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students who plan careers that engage with science and technology, as well as in business, law, and medicine.

Sociology is the study of the social lives of people, groups, and societies. Its subject matter is our own behavior as social beings. Sociology offers a distinctive and enlightening way of seeing and understanding the social world in which we live and which shapes our lives. It is the study of social structure and social change, and the causes and consequences of human behavior.

Department: The College of Arts and Sciences
